A lot of the fears expressed here aren't as bad as you'd think, especially when it comes to shared experiences. Currently VR offers many different ways to watch content, however many people choose to arguably experience that content in lower quality with more noise and potential lag purely so they can experience it with other people in apps like VRChat or BigScreen. The desire for people to have shared experiences and the ability to do so won't disappear with AR and VR glasses, it will instead make the world even more connected and make it far easier to have shared experiences with other people. At the same time, those people that are more introverted and don't want to be surrounded by other people will also have a safe space of their own to relax if wanted.

The isolation argument is just nonsense. As an early adopter of VR since the very first consumer shipment of the HTC Vive I have demo'd VR to pretty much everyone I know. Ive had my entire living room filled with people playing VR through mixed device games and passing the headset waiting for our turns just like when we were kids with the nintendo taking turns to beat each others scores. Now I have the Quest 3 and like the AVP it has full video passthrough allowing the user to see the room they are in negating the only real isolation of VR being in a headset you cant see people, thats no longer a problem, I just walk around the house with my headset on interacting with everyone the same as if I wasnt wearing it. Mixed reality games like the cabin are a ton of fun for everyone watching because they are in the video seeing the zombies in the room with them, its quite the unique experience to now demo mixed realty to people for the first time.
